name: Nasal Polyps
preview_text: The key to lasting relief from nasal polyps lies in identifying whether the root is Qi deficiency, phlegm-dampness, or inflammation - and treating that, not just the growth. When t...
synonyms: ["Nasal Growths", "Polyps In The Nose", "Polyps In Nasal Cavity", "Polyp Inside Nose", "Nasal Po", "Nasosinusal Polyposis", "Nasal Polypoid", "Nasal Polyp Disease", "Polyps In Nose"]
conventional_description: Nasal polyps are soft, painless, noncancerous growths that form on the lining of the nasal passages or sinuses. They result from chronic inflammation of the mucous membrane and are often associated with conditions like asthma, allergies, recurrent infections, or aspirin sensitivity. Typical symptoms include persistent nasal congestion, a reduced or lost sense of smell, a runny nose, postnasal drip, and facial pressure. Diagnosis is usually made through nasal endoscopy, sometimes with a CT scan to assess the extent.
conventional_treatments: Standard Western treatment typically starts with corticosteroid nasal sprays to shrink polyps and reduce inflammation. Oral corticosteroids may be used for short-term flare-ups. If medications are insufficient, surgery - such as polypectomy or endoscopic sinus surgery - is often performed. For severe, recurrent cases, biologic medications like dupilumab may be prescribed. However, polyps frequently recur after surgery if the underlying inflammation persists.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the nose is the opening of the Lungs, so any chronic nasal problem is seen as a reflection of Lung function. But the whole picture involves more than just the Lungs. The Spleen transforms and transports fluids, and when it's weak, dampness and phlegm can accumulate. The Kidneys govern water metabolism and anchor the Qi that the Lungs breathe in - a Kidney weakness can allow phlegm to drift upward and settle in the nose.
Polyps are essentially a form of congealed phlegm-dampness. If the body's Qi is strong and fluids move freely, this accumulation doesn't happen. But when there's a deficiency (Spleen, Lung, or Kidney) or an obstruction (heat, phlegm, blood stasis), the normal flow is disrupted. The excess fluid thickens and sticks, gradually forming the soft, pale growths we call polyps.
That's why the same Western diagnosis can have very different TCM roots. One person's polyps may be linked to chronic fatigue and weak digestion (Spleen-Lung Qi Deficiency), while another's may flare after every cold (Wind-Heat invading the Lungs), and a third's may be dark, firm, and prone to bleeding (Blood Stasis with Heat). Each root requires a different treatment strategy - tonifying, clearing, or moving - not just a one-size-fits-all approach.
classical_quote: 「肺气通于鼻，肺脏为风冷所乘，则鼻气不和，津液壅塞，而为鼻息肉。」
classical_translation: "The Lung Qi communicates with the nose. When the Lung is attacked by wind-cold, the nasal Qi becomes disharmonious, fluids stagnate and block, and nasal polyps form."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 29, Section on Nasal Disorders 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner starts by asking about the quality of the nasal blockage and any discharge, then looks at your energy, digestion, and body signs. The feel of the pulse and the appearance of the tongue are essential clues, because each pattern behind nasal polyps leaves a distinct fingerprint in these areas.
If fatigue, frequent colds, a pale face, and clear or white watery nasal discharge dominate, Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency is likely. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak and thready. The polyps are usually soft and pale, and symptoms worsen with overwork.
When the nose produces thick, sticky, and copious mucus, and you feel a heavy sensation in the head and chest, Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs is the main driver. The tongue coating is thick and greasy, the pulse is slippery, and the polyps look boggy and swollen. This pattern often coexists with digestive sluggishness.
A more acute, irritable picture-yellow discharge, an itchy nose, sneezing, and perhaps a mild fever or facial redness-points to Wind-Heat invading the Lungs. The tongue is red with a thin yellow coating, and the pulse is floating and rapid. The polyps are inflamed and tender.
In long-standing cases with lower back and knee soreness, frequent nighttime urination, and a deep sense of cold, Kidney Qi Deficiency may be the root. The tongue is pale and the pulse is deep and weak. The nasal symptoms are stubborn and tend to recur, with a clear or thin discharge.
When the polyps feel firm, look dark, or bleed easily, and the complexion is dull or dark, Blood Stagnation with Heat is present. The tongue is purplish with a yellow coat, and the pulse feels choppy. This pattern often emerges after years of chronic inflammation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen and Lungs are weak, they fail to transform and transport fluids properly. This leads to an accumulation of dampness and phlegm, which congeals in the nasal passages and gradually forms soft, pale polyps. Because the body's defensive Qi is also weak, you may catch colds easily, and each infection adds more dampness, making the polyps grow or return.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a thin white slippery coating. Pulse: weak and forceless, especially deficient in the right cun (Lung) and right guan (Spleen) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Qi is easily damaged by cold and raw foods, overwork, and mental strain, which then fails to control dampness. Lung Qi is weakened by cold air and repeated infections, losing its ability to keep the nose clear. Rest, warmth, and gentle movement conserve and rebuild Qi, while steam directly moistens and opens the nasal passages, giving temporary relief as the underlying deficiency is corrected.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congee, and avoid raw, cold, or greasy items that weaken the Spleen. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi builds Qi without exhausting you. Keep the nose and neck warm in cold weather, and use a humidifier or steam inhalation to keep nasal passages clear. Manage worry and overthinking, as these emotions directly weaken the Spleen.

patterns.why_this_happens:
In TCM, the Lungs open into the nose. When the Lungs are burdened by Dampness and Phlegm, the normal downward flow of Lung Qi is disrupted and the excess fluid congeals into sticky mucus. This pathological Phlegm-Dampness rises and settles in the nasal passages, causing the chronic swelling and tissue overgrowth that form polyps.
The root of the problem often lies in a weak Spleen that fails to transform and transport fluids, allowing Dampness to accumulate. This Dampness then collects in the Lungs, creating a cycle of congestion and obstruction that makes the nose feel perpetually heavy and blocked.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks and a thick, white, greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), often with a soggy quality, and particularly full in the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Phlegm is a heavy, sticky pathogen that thrives in cool, humid environments and is directly worsened by foods that create more Dampness, such as dairy, cold raw foods, and overeating. A sluggish lifestyle further congeals fluids. Warmth, both from the environment and from cooked, spiced foods, dries Dampness and helps the Spleen transform fluids. Steam inhalation physically moistens and then drains the nasal passages, mimicking the drying action of aromatic herbs, while gentle exercise moves Qi, which is essential for draining accumulated Dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods as well as dairy, which are notoriously damp-producing. Focus on warm, cooked meals like soups and congees with a little ginger. Steaming the face over a bowl of hot water with a towel over the head can help open the nasal passages and dry local dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking supports the Spleen and keeps Qi flowing.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Kidneys govern water metabolism and anchor the Qi that the Lungs breathe in. When Kidney Qi is weak, the body cannot properly transform and transport fluids, allowing phlegm-dampness to form and drift upward. This dampness settles in the nasal passages and, over time, congeals into the soft, pale growths we call nasal polyps.
Because the Kidneys are the root of all Yang energy, this deficiency also weakens the Lungs' ability to keep the nose clear, making polyps slow to resolve and prone to recurrence.

patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Qi is depleted by overwork, cold, and emotional strain, especially fear. Rest, warmth, and nourishing foods rebuild this root energy, allowing the body to properly manage fluids and prevent dampness from accumulating in the nose. Gentle movement keeps Qi flowing without further draining the Kidneys.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees are your allies. Include kidney-nourishing ingredients such as black beans, walnuts, and lamb. Avoid raw, cold, and icy foods that further weaken Kidney Qi. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps circulate Qi without depleting it.

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling and blood-moving foods like eggplant, hawthorn, and a little vinegar; avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods that add heat. faqs.question: Can acupuncture really shrink nasal polyps?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can help reduce polyp size by improving local circulation, reducing inflammation, and addressing the underlying imbalance that allowed the polyp to form. Points like Yingxiang (LI-20) directly target the nasal passages, while distal points strengthen the Lungs, Spleen, or Kidneys depending on your pattern. Results are gradual and best when combined with herbal medicine.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: No. Herbal formulas are typically taken for several weeks to months until the polyps shrink and symptoms stabilize. Once the underlying imbalance is corrected, many people stop daily herbs and may only use them during flare-ups or seasonally. Your practitioner will adjust the plan as you improve.

faqs.question: Can TCM help after polyp surgery?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM is excellent for post-surgical recovery - it can reduce inflammation, speed healing, and most importantly, address the root cause to prevent recurrence. Many patients use acupuncture and herbs after surgery to maintain clear sinuses long-term.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe if I'm using corticosteroid nasal sprays?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can generally be used alongside corticosteroid sprays. There are no known major interactions, but always inform both your TCM practitioner and your ENT doctor about all treatments. As your symptoms improve, your doctor may adjust the spray dosage - never stop prescribed medications abruptly without consulting them.

faqs.question: How long until I can breathe better?
faqs.answer: Many people notice improved nasal airflow within 2-4 weeks of starting acupuncture and herbs. Actual polyp shrinkage takes longer - typically 6-12 weeks for noticeable reduction. The timeline depends on your pattern and how long the polyps have been present.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid dairy products, greasy or fried foods, and cold raw foods - these all promote dampness and phlegm. Sugar and refined carbohydrates can also contribute. Favor warm, cooked meals with spices like ginger and garlic, which help dry excess dampness. For pattern-specific dietary advice, see the individual pattern tabs.

faqs.question: Does TCM work for all types of nasal polyps?
faqs.answer: TCM is most effective for inflammatory polyps linked to chronic sinusitis or allergies. It may be less effective for very large, obstructive polyps that require surgical removal. Even then, TCM can help prevent regrowth. A thorough evaluation will determine if TCM is appropriate for your case.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic rhinosinusitis: a systematic review
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review assessed acupuncture as an adjunctive treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis, including patients with nasal polyps. The review found limited high-quality evidence but noted that acupuncture may improve quality of life and reduce congestion when added to usual care.
research.periodical: Kim SY, Kim JI, Lee H, et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015;Issue 11. Art. No.: CD011994.
